newsitem.title: USA: Illinois seen short on electricity this summer.
newsitem.headline: Illinois seen short on electricity this summer.

text.p: Portions of the U.S. Midwest could see a summer power crunch with potential electricity outages due to shutdowns at some of the region's biggest power generation facilities, industry officials said.

Illinois and Wisconsin, both within the Mid-American Interpool Network (MAIN) electricity distribution region, could be caught short of power during any heat wave and customers may potentially lose service, the officials said.
"They are looking at a high probability of some reliability problems," said analyst Lawrence Nakovich, a director at Cambridge Energy Research Association.
Demand for electricity could surge if hot weather has Midwesterners drawing heavily on air conditioners, and limited power supply may not be able to keep up, the sources said.
"Throw a hot summer in there and you could be looking at double digit increases in power usage," Nakovich said.

Commonwealth Edison Co (ComEd), which supplies power to Illinois and Wisconsin, said it expects a significant portion of its nuclear power generation to be idled through the summer peak demand period.

Eight of ComEd's 12 Illinois nuclear power units are currently off line for refueling and repairs, and while the company expects to return four of those to service by early June, four units are also expected to remain idled.

ComEd, a subsidiary of Unicom Corp, has a total nuclear generation capacity of about 11,852 megawatts (MW), of which 4,236 MW, or about 36 percent of the company's nuclear capacity, will remain shut into next year as the Zion and Lasalle nuclear power plants undergo extensive overhauls.
Combined with several nuclear outages in Wisconsin, power supplies in the area are expected to be tight, but ComEd has said it should be able to meet summer demand without any significant problems.
"Short of losing another unit or having another 100-year heat wave, we're pretty confident we won't have any problem meeting demand," said ComEd spokesman Art Massa.

Massa said the company has been offering financial incentives to customers in exchange for agreements that power can be cut to businesses with two hours notice and will be reduced by residential consumers during hot weather.
Fuel oil and natural gas-fired "peaking" generation units, which are more expensive to run than nuclear or coal-fired units, are also being readied for service during high demand periods, Massa said.
On average, about 50 percent of ComEd's generation will come from coal-fired sources, with the remaining 50 percent coming from nuclear power, Massa said.
But analysts said ComEd's austerity programs may not be enough if Illinois and Wisconsin are hit by a week of 100-degree Fahrenheit temperatures.
"Even if we have a normal summer they are going to be surprised," Nakovich said. "You've got an economy that is continuing to grow, and with it power demand."

Compounding any supply shortage would be nuclear outages in Wisconsin, where Wisconsin Energy Corp's two Point Beach nuclear units, each rated at 485 MW, are not expected to return to service from their maintenance and refueling outages until late June and early July, the analyst said.
Importing power may also prove difficult, with transmission contraints common into western Illinois from such cheap-power states as Minnesota and Iowa.

Wholesale power for the peak summer months in MAIN has been commanding relatively high prices, with brokers and marketers trading July/August peak power into ComEd at $32.60-33.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) on Tuesday.
By comparison, July/August peak power into the Entergy system in Louisiana, where summer peak demand is also typically strong, was talked at $28.40-28.75 per MWh on Tuesday.
Currently peak, next-day spot power into ComEd is being discussed at the $19.50-20.25 level.
((--New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1627))
